Albertina Sisulu was a nurse long before she was a symbol. She trained in Johannesburg, worked in clinics and wards, and joined the African National Congress Women's League in the 1940s. Over the decades that followed she was banned, detained and watched, while her husband Walter sat in prison, and she raised a family and kept a movement alive. In 1983 she became one of the co-presidents of the United Democratic Front.

Here is the detail worth holding on to. By the time the cameras found Albertina Sisulu, she had spent decades doing the work. The title was the last thing to arrive, not the first.

Today is the second EPIC day, and the pillar is Purpose Driven. Purpose, in the EPIC framework, is the answer to a simple question: why do you do what you do? Real purpose is older than the campaign. It shows up in how a person spent their time before anybody was counting.
Compare that with this season. Posters appear on every lamp post. Candidates arrive in streets they have not visited in five years, shake hands at taxi ranks and promise a clinic, a tarred road, a park. Some of that is sincere. Much of it is scheduling. Purpose that appears only when votes are on the line is not purpose. It is a diary entry.

Charlotte Maxeke is the clearest counter-example in our history. She built the Bantu Women's League and organised in Bloemfontein and beyond, decades before anyone offered her a platform. She never held a vote or a seat in government. She held a reason, and the reason was enough to carry her across a lifetime.

What can an ordinary voter do with this? 

Ask the purpose question in a form you can check.
Ask what this candidate was doing in your community five years ago. Not in the province, not in the party, but in your ward. Were they at the community meeting when the water went off? Did they sit on a school governing body, a street committee, a community policing forum, a burial society? Ask people who live near them, not their campaign team.

Ask why this candidate wants the job. Listen for the difference between a reason and a ranking. A reason sounds like a specific problem in a specific place that the person cannot stop thinking about. A ranking sounds like ambition: leadership, position, a salary, a seat.

Ask whether the candidate has read the municipality's Integrated Development Plan, the five-year plan that sets out what the council is meant to deliver. Every municipality must have one, and it should be available from the council or on its website. If a candidate asks for your vote to run a municipality whose plan they have never read, they are asking you to trust a stranger with a document they cannot discuss.

None of this requires a degree. Ask three people who know the candidate what they have actually done for the community. Their answers beat any poster.

Sisulu and Maxeke did not wait to be invited. They saw a need and started where they stood. That is the standard for those who ask to lead us. The ward you live in has a hundred small problems that nobody has put on a poster. The person who can name them, and who was working on them before the campaign began, has already shown you something that no manifesto can.

Before you vote, ask what your candidate was doing in your community before the election was called.

Character first. Then the Ballot.

GCV Pioneer Community Education Series #137
Reason and Responsibility: How to Build a Better Future in Times of Crisis

From Social Unrest in France to National Fiscal Challenges and the Development of the Pi Network Ecosystem
Author: Doris Yin

We all want a better life. We want governments to provide better social benefits and society to create more opportunities for us. But we must also ask ourselves: Where does wealth come from? Where does government money come from? If everyone wants more but no one is willing to accept responsibility and create value, how long can society continue to prosper?

A nation's prosperity cannot depend on benefits and redistribution alone. It also requires productivity, hard work, and the contributions of every member of society.

France is a high-welfare country. In the past, when economic development, productivity, and social security could support one another, its welfare system had a sound foundation and provided protection for many citizens.

However, times are changing. An aging population, slower growth in the working-age population, and insufficient economic growth are creating new challenges for the existing welfare system. A system that was sustainable in the past may not remain sustainable under changing conditions without adjustments.

In the face of these realities, we need rational analysis, shared responsibility, and practical solutions—not endless blame and division.

1. Social Unrest in France: How Can We Express Our Concerns While Accepting Social Responsibility?
I understand that people have their own concerns and the right to express dissatisfaction. However, we must recognize one important principle: even when our demands are justified, we must consider how we pursue them and what consequences our actions may bring.

Large demonstrations can escalate emotionally. They may also be exploited by individuals with ulterior motives or by opportunists seeking to take advantage of the situation. The original demands can be overshadowed by violence, and peaceful demonstrations can deteriorate into vandalism and looting.

When shops, supermarkets, luxury boutiques, public buildings, and historical sites are damaged, we must ask ourselves: Who ultimately bears the cost?

First, businesses suffer, and ordinary people suffer with them.

When shops are looted or vandalized, business owners face not only the loss of merchandise but also repair expenses, security costs, business interruptions, and lost revenue.

If companies no longer consider a location safe for business, they may reduce investment, close stores, or move their operations elsewhere.

Supermarkets provide food and daily necessities to local residents. If stores close or leave, shopping becomes less convenient. For people who are already struggling financially, life becomes even more difficult.

Second, tourism and a city's reputation can also suffer.

France has a rich cultural heritage, historic architecture, and world-famous tourist destinations. Visitors come to experience its history and culture, not to encounter damaged buildings, shattered storefronts, and chaotic streets.

If violence and destruction continue, tourists may cancel their trips, and hotels, restaurants, shops, and tour operators may lose business. Employment opportunities can also be affected.

Historic buildings can require enormous sums to repair once damaged, and some losses cannot easily be reversed.

Third, governments must spend money repairing damaged public infrastructure.

Schools, roads, public buildings, and other infrastructure require funding when they are damaged.

Yet governments may already be facing fiscal pressure. If they must spend additional money on repairs, cleanup, and security, the financial burden becomes even heavier.

This creates a vicious cycle: the weaker the economy becomes, the less money the government has; the less money the government has, the harder it becomes to address public needs; and further economic destruction only makes the situation worse.

If our goal is to improve people's lives, we should seek solutions rather than destroy the foundations that allow society to function.

2. France's High-Welfare System: Where Does the Money Come From?
France has long maintained an extensive welfare system. A high level of social welfare is not inherently a problem. When the economy generates sufficient resources and society can afford the associated costs, a strong welfare system can protect people's living standards and contribute to social stability.

The challenge is that a welfare system must be supported by the continuous creation of wealth.

When a country has a relatively young population, a sufficient workforce, strong economic growth, and rising productivity, more workers can contribute through employment, taxes, and social security payments to support pensions, healthcare, education, and other public services.

However, when the population ages, the number of retirees increases, the working-age population grows more slowly, and economic growth and productivity gains are insufficient to support rising public expenditure, the existing welfare system faces increasing pressure.

More people need pensions and public services, while the number of people creating wealth, paying taxes, and supporting social security may grow more slowly or decline relative to those receiving benefits. When the wealth a country produces is insufficient to support its existing commitments, fiscal pressure becomes increasingly apparent.

This does not mean that high welfare is inherently wrong. It means we must face reality: every welfare system requires a sufficiently strong economic foundation.

If the wealth created by society grows slowly while public expenditure continues to rise, governments must seriously consider how to improve productivity, expand the economy, increase employment, and maintain sustainable public finances.

France's fiscal challenges are also connected to public debt, budget deficits, economic competitiveness, demographic changes, and government spending. They cannot be attributed to a single cause.

Some people may question the government's fiscal priorities, arguing that substantial amounts of money have been directed toward defense or support for Ukraine. These are government policy decisions. I will not make unwarranted judgments about them or presume to determine the merits of every individual decision.

However, one point must be clear: defense spending serves a long-term purpose. It is necessary to protect national security, safeguard citizens' lives and property, and defend a country's interests.

A country cannot focus exclusively on immediate social benefits while ignoring its long-term security. Building and maintaining defense capabilities often requires sustained investment. A nation cannot wait until a serious security threat emerges before beginning to prepare.

As for money already spent in the past, whether on defense or other public expenditure, those decisions have already been made and the money has already been spent. We cannot turn back time, nor can we expect every past expenditure to be recovered.

Therefore, instead of endlessly dwelling on the past, we should seriously consider what needs to be done next.

The past has already happened. What matters now is looking forward, improving national governance, revitalizing the economy, making public finances more sustainable, and improving people's lives.

Governments must allocate spending responsibly, and society must understand the realities a country faces. Fiscal challenges cannot be solved simply by cutting one category of expenditure while ignoring deeper problems such as insufficient productivity, population aging, and sluggish economic growth.

If the economy develops sustainably, businesses are willing to invest, and workers create more value, government revenues can improve and the welfare system can gain a stronger foundation.

3. Even the Best Cook Cannot Make a Meal Without Rice
There is a Chinese saying: Even the most capable cook cannot prepare a meal without rice.

No matter how skilled a cook may be, without rice, there is no rice to cook.

Likewise, even if a government wants to improve education, expand welfare, increase pensions, maintain national defense, and repair public infrastructure, it must have sufficient financial resources.

If economic growth is inadequate and government revenue is limited while public expenditure continues to increase, the government will face difficult choices.

If we want better healthcare, better education, more reliable pensions, and safer living conditions, we must consider how to create enough wealth to support these goals.

Without rice, we can grow more, buy more, or increase production. But if we destroy the kitchen as well, how are we supposed to prepare a meal?

A country needs stable businesses, hardworking people, sustained investment, technological innovation, and higher productivity. Only when the economic foundation becomes stronger can governments gain greater capacity to protect people's livelihoods.

We cannot focus only on how much money the government should spend. We must also consider how much wealth society actually produces and how much more it can generate in the future.

4. Population Aging and Retirement: We Must Share the Responsibility
Another long-term challenge facing France is population aging and the growing pressure on pension expenditure.

As the number of retirees increases while the working-age population grows more slowly or declines, society must confront a fundamental question: the number of people creating wealth, paying taxes, and contributing to pension systems may shrink relative to the number of people receiving pensions.

If everyone wants to retire earlier while also demanding higher pensions and better public services, we must ask:

Who will work? Who will create wealth? Who will contribute to the pension system?

Young people face their own financial pressures. They must pay for housing, raise children, support their families, and contribute through their work and social security payments to the wider system.

If there are not enough workers and productivity does not improve, the burden on younger generations may become increasingly heavy.

Therefore, we must rethink the relationship between work, retirement, and social responsibility.

There is a Chinese saying: “Diligence leads to prosperity.”

Hard work means making an effort to create wealth through employment, production, and innovation. For people who are able to work and whose health permits, extending their working lives where appropriate and increasing workforce participation can raise economic output and help ease pressure on pension systems.

Retirement policies must also account for differences in occupations, working conditions, and individual health. Nevertheless, in an aging society, we must seriously discuss retirement ages, workforce participation, and how to make pension systems more sustainable.

We cannot focus only on how early we would like to retire while completely ignoring who will support us financially after retirement.

If everyone wants to retire early but there are not enough people continuing to work, how can younger generations sustain an increasingly demanding pension system?

This is not a conflict between young and old. It is a shared responsibility that society must address together.

We must protect the well-being of older people while preserving a sustainable economic future for younger generations.

5. National Prosperity Requires Shared Responsibility: Moving Forward Together
When a country faces fiscal and economic challenges, we should not remain trapped in endless arguments about the past or constant accusations against one another.

Governments have a responsibility to develop sound fiscal policies, improve the business environment, enhance governance, and create the conditions for economic growth.

Businesses have a responsibility to invest, innovate, and create employment.

Workers have a responsibility to work diligently, improve their skills, and create value.

Members of society also need to understand the challenges their country faces and consider the long-term interests of the whole community while protecting their own rights.

Defense, education, healthcare, pensions, and infrastructure all require resources. We must address people's immediate needs while preparing for the nation's future.

There is a well-known Chinese saying:

“The rise and fall of the nation is the responsibility of every citizen.”

Its meaning is clear: a nation's future is not solely the responsibility of its government. It is also closely connected to the actions of every citizen.

When a country faces difficulties, we should unite, work hard, improve productivity, support economic development, and seek solutions together.

We cannot change what has already happened, but through our actions today, we can shape what happens tomorrow.

Instead of endlessly arguing over who was right or wrong in the past, we should focus our energy on making the country stronger, revitalizing the economy, and improving people's security and quality of life.

True responsibility means not merely demanding that others change, but starting with ourselves and creating greater value for society.

6. Pi Network Is No Different: Everyone Must Participate in Building the Ecosystem
The same principle applies to the development of the Pi Network ecosystem.

Some Pioneers constantly ask when Pi will increase in value, when the ecosystem will mature, and when others will create opportunities for them. Yet they are unwilling to learn, use Pi, support merchants, participate in application development, or engage in real economic activity.

They want a prosperous ecosystem but are unwilling to help build it. They want others to create value while they simply wait to benefit.

If everyone wants to receive value but no one is willing to create it, how can the ecosystem grow?

An ecosystem needs users, merchants, developers, applications, and real economic activity. Only when more people participate, provide goods and services, and establish practical use cases can the ecosystem continue to develop.

This principle is closely connected to the development of a national economy.

A country needs workers, entrepreneurs, investors, and innovators. The Pi Network ecosystem needs users, merchants, developers, and builders.

Pi Network offers people new economic opportunities. To turn these opportunities into real momentum for ecosystem development, Pioneers must learn actively, participate, support merchants, promote practical applications, and create value through concrete actions.

Opportunities become results only when combined with action. An ecosystem grows only when people work together to build it.

We cannot spend all our time waiting for others to create opportunities while doing nothing ourselves.

7. True Wisdom: Accept Responsibility and Build a Better Future
I have always believed that a wise person must learn to see the bigger picture rather than focus exclusively on immediate personal interests.

We can express our concerns, ask governments to improve public services, and raise objections to policies we consider unreasonable. But we must also consider the consequences of our actions and understand what a country needs for long-term development.

A country needs a stable business environment, continuous wealth creation, responsible public spending, and the understanding, hard work, and contributions of its people.

Likewise, an ecosystem can develop only when people are willing to learn, participate, and build.

A nation's prosperity requires everyone to accept responsibility. An ecosystem's growth requires everyone to participate in building it.

True progress does not come from continually demanding more from others. It comes from asking ourselves what value we can contribute to society.

We cannot change the past, but we can change our actions today and influence the direction of tomorrow.

If we want a better life, we must help create the conditions for a better life. If we want a stronger nation, we must share the responsibility of building it. If we want a better future, we must begin working toward it today.

Reason helps us understand reality. Responsibility gives us a sense of duty. Action is what truly changes the future.

That is the essence of wisdom.

— Doris Yin

Morning Call: Verdeelde Europese opening, Azië herstelt sterk en Applied Materials vergroot belang in Besi

De Europese beurzen gaan een verdeelde opening tegemoet. Wall Street herstelde maandag en Azië laat vanochtend forse winsten zien, vooral bij technologie. De Amerikaanse futures liggen echter vrijwel vlak. Het sterke herstel in Zuid-Korea en Japan biedt kansen voor Europese aandelen, maar moet hier nog door kopers worden bevestigd.

Voor Amsterdam is het belangrijkste nieuws dat Applied Materials zijn belang in Besi wil vergroten tot ongeveer 20%. Dat bevestigt de strategische waarde van Besi, maar vermindert tegelijkertijd de speculatie over een snelle volledige overname. Ook Universal Music Group verdient aandacht na berichten over gesprekken met investeringsmaatschappijen.

De enorme bedragen die nodig zijn voor AI, de financiële onrust in Brazilië en de dreiging van nieuwe Amerikaanse aanvallen op Iran blijven belangrijke risico's. Vandaag staan bovendien de Israëlische verkiezingen en een volle agenda met kwartaalcijfers centraal.

Europa en futures
■ Opening Europa: Verdeeld. De Europese futures geven geen eenduidige richting aan. Het sterke herstel in Azië biedt steun, maar een positieve opening is nog niet zeker.
■ Amerikaanse futures: Vrijwel onveranderd. Na het herstel van maandag consolideert Wall Street. Er is voorlopig geen nieuwe duidelijke koopimpuls vanuit de futures.
■ AEX: Sloot maandag 0,14% hoger op 1.133,19 punten. Een herstel richting 1.140 blijft mogelijk wanneer technologie en banken steun vinden.
■ STOXX 600: Sloot maandag 0,77% hoger op 640,66 punten. Vooral defensie, banken, industrie en reizen presteerden goed. De bredere verbetering is positief voor het Europese sentiment.

Wall Street
■ S&P 500: +0,70% naar 7.676,77 punten. De Nasdaq steeg 0,82% naar 26.169,38 punten en de Dow Jones won 0,28% tot 52.361,58 punten.
■ Halfgeleiders: De Philadelphia Semiconductor Index steeg 2,8%, de grootste dagwinst in ongeveer een maand. Nvidia won 2,4%. De sterke Aziatische reactie biedt mogelijkheden voor een vervolg van het herstel.
■ Marktbeeld: Zeven van de elf sectoren binnen de S&P 500 sloten hoger. Technologie en industrie waren sterk, terwijl communicatie en defensieve consumentengoederen achterbleven. Dat wijst op een herstel dat breder wordt gedragen dan uitsluitend door AI-aandelen.

Azië
■ MSCI Azië exclusief Japan: Circa 1,2% hoger. Het herstel wordt vooral gedragen door technologie.
■ Zuid-Korea: De Kospi stijgt ongeveer 3,6%. SK Hynix wint circa 7% en Samsung Electronics bijna 5%. Beleggers kijken vooruit naar de kwartaalcijfers en de vooruitzichten voor geheugenprijzen.
■ Japan: De Nikkei stijgt ongeveer 2%. Advantest wint meer dan 10% en SoftBank circa 7%. Vooral bedrijven die actief zijn rond AI en geavanceerde chips profiteren.
■ China en Hongkong: Blijven achter. De Hang Seng verliest ongeveer 0,2% en Shanghai noteert licht lager. De markt wacht op mogelijke economische maatregelen vanuit Beijing.

Belangrijkste aandelen en bedrijfsnieuws
■ Applied Materials en Besi: Applied Materials heeft een overeenkomst gesloten om zijn belang in Besi te verhogen van ongeveer 9% naar 20%. De transactie moet nog worden goedgekeurd. De samenwerking tussen beide bedrijven, die in 2020 begon, wordt verder uitgebreid op het gebied van hybrid bonding en nieuwe verbindingstechnologie voor chips. Applied Materials benadrukt voorlopig niet verder dan 20% te willen gaan en geen bestuurszetel na te streven. Dat is positief voor de strategische positie van Besi, maar vermindert de verwachtingen van een snelle volledige overname. Voor vandaag wordt vooral de koersreactie belangrijk. Een hogere waardering door de strategische samenwerking is mogelijk, maar een directe overnamepremie ligt minder voor de hand.
■ Universal Music Group: Volgens Bloomberg heeft het bedrijf eerder dit jaar verkennende gesprekken gevoerd met Apollo, TPG en Blackstone over een mogelijke beursafgang. Er is geen formeel verkoopproces gestart en Reuters kon het bericht niet onafhankelijk bevestigen. Toch kan het nieuws belangstelling voor het aandeel aanwakkeren. Vooral de waarde van de muziekcatalogus en het verschil tussen publieke en private waarderingen zijn interessant.
■ Apple: Het bedrijf erkent problemen met het binnenste scherm van een beperkt aantal nieuwe iPhone Duo-toestellen. Apple biedt getroffen klanten vervangende toestellen aan. Het is nog niet duidelijk of de problemen op grotere schaal voorkomen. Voorlopig lijkt het risico beperkt, maar de duurzaamheid van het scherm kan belangrijk worden voor het succes van de nieuwe productcategorie.
■ Anthropic: Heeft officieel een aanvraag ingediend voor een Amerikaanse beursgang. De omzet over de eerste helft van 2026 bedroeg $16,3 miljard. Het nettoverlies kwam uit op $80,7 miljard, waarvan ruim $72 miljard verband hield met een boekhoudkundige herwaardering van converteerbare leningen. Het operationele verlies bedroeg $693 miljoen. De beursgang wordt een belangrijke test voor de waardering van AI-bedrijven en de bereidheid van beleggers om toekomstige groei te financieren.
■ Anthropic en Broadcom: Bank of America, Citi, Morgan Stanley en Blackstone hebben een financiering van $63 miljard aangekondigd voor de aankoop van chips en netwerkapparatuur van Broadcom. De apparatuur wordt via een afzonderlijke onderneming aan Anthropic verhuurd. Broadcom biedt de financiers bescherming tegen waardeverlies van de apparatuur. De vraag naar AI blijft sterk, maar dergelijke constructies vergroten ook de financiële afhankelijkheid tussen leveranciers, klanten en kredietverstrekkers.
■ Meta Platforms: Wil tot $95 miljard aan nieuw aandelenkapitaal ophalen voor verdere AI-investeringen. De eerste uitgifte bedraagt ongeveer $35 miljard, gevolgd door een mogelijk aanvullend programma van maximaal $60 miljard. Nvidia, AMD en Broadcom hebben belangstelling getoond om gezamenlijk tot $5 miljard te investeren. De financiering biedt ruimte voor groei, maar kan bestaande aandeelhouders verwateren. De markt zal vooral kijken naar het rendement op deze enorme investeringen.
■ SpaceX: Een aan Apollo verbonden partij gaat voor ongeveer $40 miljard aan chips en servers kopen en deze vervolgens aan SpaceX verhuren. Ook hier blijkt hoe groot de behoefte aan externe financiering is geworden. Het verschil tussen bedrijven die gemakkelijk kapitaal kunnen aantrekken en ondernemingen met oplopende financieringskosten wordt steeds belangrijker.
■ Brazilië: De Bovespa verloor maandag 13,9%, de grootste dagdaling sinds maart 2020. De Braziliaanse real daalde 8,1% tegenover de dollar en de ETF EWZ verloor bijna 20%. Ook de obligatiemarkt stond onder zware druk. Beleggers vrezen hogere overheidsuitgaven na de herverkiezing van Lula. Voor vandaag wordt belangrijk of de markt stabiliseert en of er duidelijkheid komt over het toekomstige begrotingsbeleid. Ook Europese bedrijven met grote Braziliaanse activiteiten blijven gevoelig voor nieuwe koersbewegingen.
■ HSBC: De winst voor belastingen steeg in het derde kwartaal met 32% naar $9,6 miljard. De bank kondigde een aandeleninkoop van maximaal $1 miljard aan en de verwachte kredietverliezen daalden. De resultaten bieden enige steun aan het sentiment rond Europese banken.
■ EQT en Range Resources: EQT neemt Range Resources over voor ongeveer $13 miljard in aandelen. De combinatie krijgt een ondernemingswaarde van ruim $50 miljard en wordt de grootste aardgasproducent van de Verenigde Staten. De overname bevestigt dat energiebedrijven rekening houden met een structureel hogere vraag naar aardgas vanuit elektriciteitscentrales, LNG en datacenters.
■ Pharming en overige cijfers: Pharming publiceert vanochtend cijfers. Ook Novartis, Porsche, Beiersdorf, Orange, Boeing, Coca-Cola, UPS en PayPal staan op de agenda. Vanavond volgen onder meer ASMI, NXP en Visa. Vooral de verwachtingen voor de komende kwartalen kunnen grote koersbewegingen veroorzaken.
Sectoren Europa
■ Halfgeleiders: Voorzichtig positief door het sterke herstel in Azië. De cijfers van grote technologiebedrijven later deze week worden bepalend.
■ Geheugen en AI-hardware: De vraag blijft sterk, maar de markt kijkt kritischer naar marges, investeringen en financiering.
■ Optische netwerken: Positieve vooruitzichten door de verdere uitbreiding van datacenters. De financiële positie van klanten verdient wel meer aandacht.
■ Software en cloud: Microsoft en Alphabet moeten woensdag bevestigen dat de groei van hun cloudactiviteiten de hoge AI-investeringen rechtvaardigt.
■ Banken: De resultaten van HSBC bieden steun. Banken met grote belangen in Brazilië blijven kwetsbaar.
■ Gezondheidszorg: Relatief defensief. De komende resultaten van grote farmaciebedrijven kunnen voor nieuwe kansen zorgen.
■ Auto-industrie: Voorzichtig. Porsche publiceert cijfers en de zwakke Chinese vraag blijft een belangrijk risico.
■ Luchtvaart en transport: Een verdere daling van Brentolie kan de sector ondersteunen. UPS geeft vandaag meer inzicht in de internationale vervoersmarkt.
■ Olie en gas: Lagere olieprijzen kunnen tijdelijk op de koersen drukken. De overname van Range Resources bevestigt wel de belangstelling voor aardgas op langere termijn.
■ Chemie: Hoge Europese gasprijzen blijven een probleem voor de marges. Lagere energiekosten kunnen herstel ondersteunen.
■ Industrie en defensie: Investeringen in elektriciteitsnetten, infrastructuur en defensie blijven positief voor de orderportefeuilles.
■ Telecom: Orange publiceert vandaag cijfers. Marges, vrije kasstroom en investeringskosten worden bepalend.
■ Vastgoed: Stabiele obligatierentes kunnen steun bieden, maar financieringskosten blijven belangrijk.
■ Consumentengoederen en luxe: Beiersdorf en Coca-Cola geven meer inzicht in de consumentenvraag. Voor luxe blijft China een belangrijke factor.
■ Mijnbouw: De vraag naar koper blijft op lange termijn positief, maar hogere voorraden en onzekerheid over China beperken het herstel.

Rente en obligaties
■ Amerikaanse tienjaarsrente: Rond 4,99%. De rente blijft net onder 5%, wat enige steun biedt aan technologie en andere groeiaandelen.
■ Amerikaanse tweejaarsrente: Rond 4,71%. Beleggers houden rekening met een langere periode van hoge beleidsrentes.
■ Federal Reserve: Woensdag volgt het rentebesluit. Een ongewijzigde rente wordt verwacht. Vooral de uitspraken van voorzitter Kevin Warsh over december kunnen de markten bewegen.
■ ECB: Donderdag volgt het Europese rentebesluit. Hoge energieprijzen en de inflatievooruitzichten worden belangrijk.
■ Bank of Japan: Vrijdag volgt het Japanse rentebesluit. Een ongewijzigde rente wordt verwacht, maar een verhoging in december blijft mogelijk.
■ Frankrijk en Brazilië: Frankrijk blijft onder druk door begrotingsproblemen. In Brazilië lopen de financieringskosten op na de verkiezingsuitslag.
Valuta
■ EUR/USD: Rond 1,117. De dollar blijft relatief sterk in aanloop naar het Amerikaanse rentebesluit.
■ USD/JPY: Rond 157,7. De yen blijft gevoelig voor de verwachtingen rond de Japanse rente.
■ Braziliaanse real: Na de scherpe daling van maandag is een tijdelijke opleving mogelijk. Een overtuigend herstel vraagt echter om duidelijkheid over de overheidsfinanciën.

Olie en energie
■ Brentolie: Rond $115 per vat bij de vroege Reuters-peiling en licht lager. De markt reageert op nieuwe diplomatieke inspanningen rond Iran. De olieprijs blijft echter hoog.
■ WTI-olie: Rond $101 per vat. Nieuwe verstoringen van de olieaanvoer blijven een belangrijk risico.
■ Europees gas: De TTF-gasprijs sloot maandag rond €95 per MWh en bereikte tussentijds ruim €97. De hoge gasprijs blijft een risico voor de Europese industrie en de inflatie.

Goud, zilver en commodities
■ Goud: Rond $4.014 per ounce. De prijs staat licht onder druk door de sterke dollar. De Amerikaanse rente blijft bepalend voor het verdere verloop.
■ Zilver: Rond $54 per ounce. Een herstel is mogelijk, maar de industriële vraag en rente blijven belangrijk.
■ Platina: Laatste beschikbare indicatie rond $1.534 per ounce.
■ Palladium: Laatste beschikbare indicatie rond $1.049 per ounce.
■ Koper: De markt blijft gevoelig voor de Chinese economie en de ontwikkeling van de voorraden. De vraag vanuit elektriciteitsnetten en datacenters ondersteunt de vooruitzichten op langere termijn.

Crypto
■ Bitcoin: Beweegt rond $80.000. De koers probeert te stabiliseren, maar een overtuigende nieuwe stijging ontbreekt nog.
■ Ether: Rond $2.300. Het sentiment blijft afhankelijk van technologie, liquiditeit en de rente.
■ Signaal: Een herstel van technologie kan helpen, maar crypto geeft voorlopig geen zelfstandig koopsignaal.

Macro en agenda
■ Vandaag Europa: Frans consumentenvertrouwen en cijfers over de kredietverlening en geldhoeveelheid in de eurozone.
■ Vandaag Verenigde Staten: Om 13.30 uur Nederlandse tijd verschijnen de orders voor duurzame goederen. Om 15.00 uur volgen het consumentenvertrouwen en de verkoop van nieuwe woningen.
■ Woensdag: Rentebesluit Federal Reserve om 19.00 uur Nederlandse tijd. Daarnaast resultaten van Microsoft, Alphabet en verschillende Europese banken.
■ Donderdag: Rentebesluit ECB, Amerikaanse economische groei en PCE-inflatie. Ook Amazon, Shell en ING publiceren cijfers.
■ Vrijdag: Rentebesluit Bank of Japan en nieuwe Europese economische cijfers.

Geopolitiek en politiek
■ Israël: Vandaag zijn er parlementsverkiezingen. De positie van Netanyahu en de samenstelling van een nieuwe regering kunnen gevolgen hebben voor het beleid tegenover Iran. De eerste exitpolls volgen vanavond.
■ Iran: De Verenigde Staten hebben aangegeven vóór de tussentijdse verkiezingen van 3 november geen nieuwe aanvallen op Iran uit te voeren. Volgens Amerikaanse en Israëlische berichtgeving zijn militaire plannen voor de periode daarna voorbereid. Trump heeft nog geen besluit genomen over nieuwe militaire actie. Dit blijft een belangrijk risico voor olie, inflatie en aandelen.
■ Diplomatie: Saudi-Arabië, Turkije, Pakistan en Qatar proberen de spanningen met Iran te verminderen. Een akkoord is er nog niet.
■ Brazilië: Beleggers wachten op de samenstelling van het economische team van Lula en concrete begrotingsplannen. Politieke onzekerheid kan de financiële markten opnieuw raken.
■ Rusland en Oekraïne: Vandaag is rond Oleshky een tijdelijk lokaal bestand ingegaan om humanitaire hulp en evacuaties mogelijk te maken. Het gaat niet om een algemeen bestand. Elders gaat de oorlog door.

Desk-view
De Europese aandelenmarkten gaan een verdeelde opening tegemoet. Het sterke herstel in Azië is positief, maar de vrijwel vlakke Amerikaanse futures geven voorlopig geen extra impuls. De belangrijkste vraag is of Europese beleggers alsnog aansluiten bij de verbetering in technologie en de bredere markt.
Het nieuws rond Besi is strategisch positief, maar vermindert de verwachtingen van een snelle volledige overname. Tegelijkertijd bevestigen de financieringsplannen van Anthropic, Meta en SpaceX dat de vraag naar AI groot blijft, maar dat daarvoor steeds meer extern kapitaal nodig is.

Voor de komende dagen blijven de rentebesluiten, kwartaalcijfers en het verloop van de olieprijs bepalend. De verkiezingen in Israël en de mogelijke Amerikaanse beslissing over Iran na 3 november kunnen daarbij voor onverwachte bewegingen zorgen.
■ Richting: Verdeeld bij de opening, met kansen op herstel wanneer Europese technologie en banken steun vinden.
■ Positief: Sterk herstel in Azië, betere marktbreedte op Wall Street en aanhoudende vraag naar AI.
■ Negatief: Grote financieringsbehoefte bij AI, financiële onrust in Brazilië en het risico van nieuwe aanvallen op Iran.
■ Belangrijkste signaal: Europese aandelen moeten na de opening laten zien dat kopers actief blijven. Een breder herstel is overtuigender dan een stijging van slechts enkele technologiebedrijven.
■ Positieve surprise: Europese futures draaien hoger, Brentolie daalt verder en de verkoopdruk in Brazilië neemt af.
■ Negatieve surprise: Nieuwe dreigingen rond Iran, oplopende rente of tegenvallende vooruitzichten bij grote technologiebedrijven.
■ Houding: Selectief positief, maar zonder vooruit te lopen op een nieuwe stijgende trend. Eerst bevestiging vanuit de markt, daarna herstelkansen benutten.

Morning Call: Mixed European opening as Asia rebounds and Applied Materials increases its stake in Besi
European equities face a mixed opening. Wall Street recovered on Monday and Asian markets are posting strong gains this morning, particularly in technology. US futures, however, are almost unchanged. The recovery in South Korea and Japan creates opportunities for European stocks, but renewed buying interest still needs confirmation.
For Amsterdam, the most important development is Applied Materials' plan to increase its stake in Besi to approximately 20%. This confirms Besi's strategic importance but reduces expectations of an imminent full takeover. Universal Music Group also deserves attention following reports of preliminary discussions with private equity firms.
The substantial financing requirements of AI, financial turmoil in Brazil and the possibility of renewed US military action against Iran remain major risks. Israel also holds parliamentary elections today, while a busy corporate earnings calendar could generate significant share-price moves.
Europe and futures
■ European opening: Mixed. European futures do not provide a clear direction. Strong Asian gains offer support, but a positive opening is not assured.
■ US futures: Almost unchanged. Wall Street is consolidating after Monday's recovery, with no clear additional buying impulse.
■ AEX: Closed Monday 0.14% higher at 1,133.19. Recovery toward 1,140 remains possible if technology and banks find support.
■ STOXX 600: Closed 0.77% higher at 640.66. Defence, banks, industrials and travel stocks performed well. Broader participation is encouraging.
Wall Street
■ S&P 500: +0.70% to 7,676.77. The Nasdaq gained 0.82% to 26,169.38 and the Dow advanced 0.28% to 52,361.58.
■ Semiconductors: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 2.8%, its strongest daily gain in approximately a month. Nvidia advanced 2.4%. Asia's positive reaction creates potential for further recovery.
■ Market breadth: Seven of the eleven S&P 500 sectors finished higher. Technology and industrials outperformed, while communication services and consumer staples lagged. The recovery extended beyond AI stocks.
Asia
■ MSCI Asia ex-Japan: Approximately 1.2% higher, supported by the technology recovery.
■ South Korea: The Kospi gains around 3.6%. SK Hynix advances approximately 7% and Samsung Electronics almost 5%. Investors are focusing on upcoming earnings and memory pricing.
■ Japan: The Nikkei is approximately 2% higher. Advantest gains more than 10% and SoftBank about 7%. AI-related companies are leading.
■ China and Hong Kong: Underperform. The Hang Seng is down approximately 0.2%, while Shanghai is slightly lower. Investors await possible economic policy announcements from Beijing.
Key companies and corporate news
■ Applied Materials and Besi: Applied Materials has agreed to increase its stake in Besi from approximately 9% to 20%, subject to regulatory approval. Their partnership, established in 2020, is expanding in hybrid bonding and advanced semiconductor connections. Applied Materials has stated that it does not currently intend to exceed 20% ownership or seek board representation. The investment strengthens Besi's strategic position but reduces expectations of an imminent full takeover. Today's share-price reaction will be important. A higher valuation based on strategic cooperation remains possible, although an immediate takeover premium is less likely.
■ Universal Music Group: According to Bloomberg, UMG held preliminary discussions earlier this year with Apollo, TPG and Blackstone about a potential take-private transaction. No formal sale process has begun, and Reuters was unable to independently verify the report. The speculation could attract investor interest, particularly in the valuation of UMG's music catalogues.
■ Apple: The company has acknowledged inner-display problems affecting a limited number of its new iPhone Duo devices. Apple is offering replacements. The extent of the problem remains unclear.

text:
Microsoft on Monday announced a voluntary exit program for eligible employees in India, the US, the UK and Canada, offering financial support and career planning resources to those opting to leave the company, according to a blog post by the tech giant.

Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India, but it is not clear how many of them would be eligible for the voluntary exit program. Some 60,000 employees globally are eligible.

It is learnt that employees in India eligible for the voluntary exit offer will have till December 1 to decide.

The package is expected to look like a standard severance package, which includes one month of base pay for every year worked, health insurance and career transition services.

Microsoft just offered ~60,000 employees a voluntary exit package — roughly 27% of its entire workforce.

US, Canada, India, and UK. Level 70 and below in participating teams (Xbox, Windows, Copilot, Finance, HR, and parts of AI/cloud).

Decision by early December. Leave by year-end if accepted.

Not a mass layoff of 60k. It’s a big voluntary buyout while they pour money into AI infrastructure. Expected uptake is lower than the earlier retirement program.

Another clear signal of how hard tech is retooling around AI.

So often one hears politicians quoting the British Constitution as if it actually exists by way of adocumentary privilege — but it does not. It is simply an accumulation of old customs and precedents concerning parliamentary sanctions, together with a number of specific laws defining certain aspects. Since Scotland's 1320 Declaration of Arbroath was nullified by England's Treaty of Union in 1707, the oldest Written Constitution now in force is that of the United States of America. It was adopted in 1787, ratified in 1788, and effected in 1789. In that same year began the French Revolution, which abolished feudalism and ‘absolute’ monarchy in France, thereby influencing politics in much of Europe. In close to 200 years since the Revolution, France and other European States (with Britain as a noticeable exception) have adopted Written Constitutions to protect the rights and liberties of individuals — but who champions these Constitutions on behalf of the people? A popular alternative to absolute monarchy or dictatorship has been found in Republicanism. The Republic of the United States was created primarily to free the emergent nation from the despotism of Britain’s House of Hanover. Yet its citizens tend still to be fascinated by the concept of monarchy. No matter how Republican the spirit, the need for a central symbol remains. Neither a flag nor a president can fulfil this unifying role, for by virtue of the ‘party system’ presidents are always politically motivated. Republicanism was devised on the principle of fraternal status, yet an ideally classless society can never exist in an environment that promotes displays of eminence and superiority by degrees of wealth and possession. For the most part, those responsible for the United States’ morally inspired Constitution were Rosicrucians and Freemasons, notable characters such as George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, John Adams and Charles Thompson. The last, who designed the Great Seal of the United States of America, was a member of Franklin’s American Philosophical Society — a counterpart of Britain’s Invisible College. The imagery of the Seal is directly related to alchemical tradition, inherited from the allegory of the ancient Egyptian Therapeutate. The eagle, the olive branch, the arrows, and the pentagrams are all occult symbols of opposites: good and evil, male and female, war and peace, darkness and light. On the reverse (as repeated on the dollar bill) is the truncated pyramid, indicating the loss of the Old Wisdom, severed and forced underground by the Church establishment. But above this are the rays of ever-hopeful light, incorporating the ‘all-seeing eye’, used as a symbol during the French Revolution.
In establishing their Republic, the Americans could still not escape the ideal of a parallel monarchy — a central focus of non-political, patriotic attachment. George Washington was actually offered kingship, but declined because he had no immediately qualifying heritage. Instead he turned to the Royal House of Stuart. In November 1782 four Americans arrived at the San Clemente Palazzo in Florence, the residence of Charles III Stuart in exile. They were Mr Galloway of Maryland, two brothers named Sylvester from Pennsylvania, and Mr Fish, a lawyer from New York. They were taken to Charles Edward by his secretary, John Stewart. Also present was the Hon Charles Hervey-Townshend (later Britain’s ambassador to The Hague) and the Prince's future wife, Marguerite, Comtesse de Massillan. The interview — which revolved around the contemporary transatlantic dilemma — is doctimented in the US Senate archives and in the Manorwater Papers. Writers such as Sir Compton Mackenzie and Sir Charles Petrie have also described the occasion when Charles Edward Stuart was invited to become ‘King of the Americans’. Some years earlier, Charles had been similarly approached by the men of Boston, but once the War of Independence was over George Washington sent his own envoys. It would have been a great irony for the House of Hanover to lose the North American colonies to the Stuarts. But Charles declined the offer for a number of reasons, not the least of which was his lack of a legitimate male heir at the time. He knew that without a due successor the United States could easily fall to Hanover again at his death, thereby defeating the whole Independence effort. Since those days, many other radical events have taken place: the French Revolution, the Russian Revolution, two major World Wars, and a host of changes as countries have swapped one style of government for another. Meanwhile, civil and international disputes continue just as they did in the Middle Ages. They are motivated by trade, politics, religion, and whatever other banners are flown to justify the constant struggle for territorial and economic control. The Holy Roman Empire has disappeared, the German Reichs have failed, and the British Empire has collapsed. The Russian Empire fell to Communism, which has itself been disgraced and crumbled to ruin, while Capitalism teeters on the very brink of acceptability. With the Cold War now ended, America faces a new threat to her superpower status from the Pacific countries. In the meantime, the nations of Europe band together in what was once a seemingly well conceived economic community, but which is already suffering from the same pressures of individual custom and national sovereignty that beset the Holy Roman Empire. Whether nations are governed by military-style regimes or elected parliaments, by autocrats or democrats, and whether formally described as monarchist, socialist or republican, the net product is always the same: the few control the fate of the many. In situations of dictatorship this is a natural experience — but it should not be the case in a democratic institution based on the principle of majority vote. True democracy is government by the people for the people, in either direct or representative form, ignoring class distinctions and tolerating minority views. The American Constitution sets out an ideal for this form of democracy ... but, in line with other nations, there is always a large sector of the community that is not represented by the party in power. Because presidents and prime ministers are politically tied, and because political parties take their respective turns at individual helms, the inevitable result is a lack of continuity for the nations concerned. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but there is no reliable ongoing institution to champion the civil rights and liberties of people in such conditions of ever-changing leadership. Britain does, at least, retain a monarchy, but it is a politically constrained monarchy, and as such is ineffectual in performing its role as guardian of the nation. The United States, unlike Britain, has a Written Constitution — but has no one with the power to uphold its principles against successive governments who determinedly pursue their own politically vested interests. Is there an answer to the anomaly — an answer that could bring not just a ray of hope but a shining light for the future? There certainly is, but its energy relies on those in governmental service appreciating their roles as ‘representatives’ of society rather than presuming to stand at the head of society. Alongside the political administration, an appointed Constitutional champion would be empowered to keep check on any potential disparities and infringements of the Constitution that might occur. This can be achieved in the manner first envisaged by George Washington and the American Fathers. Their original plan was for a democratic Parliament combined with a working Constitutional Monarchy bound not to Parliament or the Church but to the people and their Written Constitution. The Monument to the Royal Stuarts is a memorial in St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican City State. It commemorates the last three members of the Royal House of Stuart: James FRANCIS Edward Stuart ("the Old Pretender", d. 1766), his elder son Charles Edward Stuart ("the Young Pretender" or "Bonnie Prince Charlie", d. 1788), and his younger son, Henry Benedict Stuart ("the Cardinal Duke of York", d. 1807). The Jacobites recognised these three as kings of England, Scotland and Ireland.

The marble monument is by Antonio Canova (1757–1822), the most celebrated Italian sculptor of his day. It was erected in 1819.

Description
The monument takes the form of a truncated obelisk. It carries bas relief profile portraits of the three exiled princes, and the following inscription:

IACOBO·III
IACOBI·II·MAGNAE·BRIT·REGIS·FILIO
KAROLO·EDVARDO
ET·HENRICO·DECANO·PATRVM·CARDINALIVM
IACOBI·III·FILIIS
REGIAE·STIRPIS·STVARDIAE·POSTREMIS
ANNO·M·DCCC·XIX
("To James III, son of King James II of Great Britain, to Charles Edward and to Henry, Dean of the Cardinal Fathers, sons of James III, the last of the Royal House of Stuart. 1819")
Below the inscription are two weeping angels, symbolising the lost hopes of the exiled Stuarts.

The monument to the Royal Stuarts was originally commissioned by Monsignor Angelo Cesarini, executor of the estate of Henry Benedict Stuart. Among the subscribers was King George IV, who (once the Jacobite threat to his throne had ended with the death of Cardinal Stuart in 1807) was an admirer of the Stuart legend.[1]

The monument stands towards the back of the basilica in the left aisle opposite the door from which people coming down the spiral staircase from the dome and roof exit. It is frequently adorned with flowers by Jacobite romantics.

Burials

The monument is, strictly speaking, a cenotaph, not a tomb. The three Stuarts are buried in the crypt below the basilica. James Francis Edward Stuart was buried here at his death in 1766. When Charles Edward Stuart died in 1788, he was buried in the Basilica of St Peter Apostle in Frascati. When his brother Henry Benedict Stuart died in 1807, both brothers were laid to rest next to their father in the crypt of St. Peter's. Three separate tombstones were erected.

Until 1938 the bodies of the three Stuarts were buried where the tomb of Pius XI now stands.

In that year the bodies were moved slightly further east on the left side of the crypt, to make room for Pius's tomb. In 1939 a single sarcophagus was erected over the three graves. On top of the sarcophagus is a bronze pillow on which is placed a bronze crown. On the front of the sarcophagus is the same inscription quoted above. The original tombstones, when they were recognized as Kings (James III, Charles III and Henry IX), are now in the Pontifical Scots College.

Other monuments
Opposite the monument to the Royal Stuarts in St. Peter's Basilica is a monument to Maria Clementina Sobieska, wife of James Francis Edward Stuart and mother of Charles Edward Stuart and Henry Benedict Stuart. Its inscription reads:

MARIA CLEMENTINA M. BRITANN.
FRANC. ET HIBERN. REGINA
("Maria Clementina, Queen of Great Britain, France and Ireland"[a])
Queen Christina of Sweden and Queen Charlotte of Cyprus, the only other monarchs with a memorial in the church, also lie entombed in the crypt below the basilica, with the Royal Stuarts. Queen Christina abdicated her throne in 1654 to convert to Catholicism while Queen Charlotte was illegally deposed in 1464 by her illegitimate half-brother.

text:
When Sophia Bennett agreed to give her boyfriend one final chance, she made herself a promise.

If he disappointed her again, she would walk away for good.

She had been dating Michael for four years, and the relationship had slowly become exhausting.

He forgot birthdays, cancelled plans at the last minute, and disappeared whenever they needed to have serious conversations.

Yet whenever Sophia tried to leave, he would apologize, promise to change, and remind her of everything they had shared.

She loved him.

That was the problem.

After their latest argument, Michael showed up at her apartment in Chicago carrying flowers and a small box of chocolates.

"I know I've made mistakes," he said. "But I want to fix this."

Sophia folded her arms.

"What exactly are you going to change?"

"Everything."

She almost laughed.

"That's what you said last time."

This time, however, Michael had a proposal.

He wanted them to start again, attend couples therapy, and plan their future together.

Sophia agreed, but only on one condition.

They would have three months to prove the relationship could work.

If nothing changed, they would separate peacefully.

Michael accepted immediately.

For the first few weeks, things improved.

He called when he said he would. He arrived on time for dates. He listened when Sophia spoke about her frustrations.

For the first time in months, she began imagining a future with him again.

Then, exactly six weeks into their agreement, Michael made an unexpected demand.

He wanted Sophia to quit her job.

She stared at him across the dinner table.

"Why?"

"Because my company is transferring me to Texas, and I want you to come with me."

Sophia worked as a nurse at a hospital she loved. She had spent years building her career and had recently been offered a promotion.

She explained this to Michael.

He shrugged.

"You can find another hospital."

"What about my promotion?"

"You can get another promotion somewhere else."

Sophia felt something inside her shift.

"Michael, we've been together for four years. You've never once asked me what I wanted for my future. Now that we're finally trying to fix things, you're asking me to abandon everything I've worked for."

He leaned back in his chair.

"If you really loved me, you'd make sacrifices."

Sophia didn't answer.

Instead, she asked him a question.

"Would you quit your job and move to another state if I asked you to?"

Michael looked offended.

"That's different. I'm building something important here."

"And so am I."

He shook his head.

"You're making this more difficult than it needs to be."

Sophia went home alone.

For the next two days, she barely slept.

She remembered the birthdays he had forgotten, the nights she had cried alone, and the countless times she had made herself smaller to keep the peace.

But she also remembered the good days.

The road trips. The laughter. The way he held her hand when her father was hospitalized.

She wondered whether leaving him meant throwing away something that could still be saved.

On the third evening, Michael called.

"Have you made your decision?"

Sophia took a deep breath.

"Yes."

"And?"

"I'm not quitting my job."

He sighed dramatically.

"Then I guess that tells me everything I need to know about your priorities."

For once, Sophia didn't rush to defend herself.

Instead, she asked, "What would you do if I said yes?"

"I'd know you were serious about us."

"And if I said no?"

"Then there's no point continuing this relationship."

Sophia sat quietly for a moment.

Then she said, "You're right."

Michael sounded surprised.

"What?"

"There's no point continuing a relationship where love is measured by how much of myself I'm willing to give up."

She ended the call.

For the first time in four years, she didn't wait for him to call back.

FREE, by our vow of poverty, to share the life of the poor and to use whatever resources we may have, not for our own security and comfort, but for service;
FREE, by our vow of chastity, to be men for others, in friendship and communion with all, but especially with those who share our mission of service;
FREE, by our vow of obedience, to respond to the call of Christ as made known to us by him whom the Spirit has placed over the Church, and to follow the lead of all our superiors.[2] [1] See GC 32, d. 4, no. 16; see GC 31, d. 16, no. 4; d. 17, no. 2; d. 18, no. 3. [2] GC 32, d. 2, no. 20. 215

On November 5, 1775, George Washington Banned Boston’s Annual Pope Night for Being Anti-Catholic
November 5, 2023
In the 18th century, the annual Pope’s Day holiday in Boston every November 5 was a chilling demonstration of the deep-seeded anti-Catholic sentiments prevalent in New England in the decades leading up to the Revolutionary War.

One of those bizarre and archaic pastimes that measure a lack of progress in the human condition, Pope’s Day was an English celebration marking a failed Catholic plot by Guy Fawkes to blow up the British Parliament in 1605. It was enthusiastically marked in England and in other places where the English gathered, and by the 1740s had become an annual tradition in Boston.

Gangs of working class men from the South End and the North End marched from their respective neighborhoods into the center of Boston, holding Effigies of the Pope and the Devil that had been studiously constructed by townspeople. Upon meeting, the two sides, fueled by rum and the excitement of old grudges, attempted to destroy the other side’s effigies. Large scale brawls were common, and occasionally one of the participants died.

The Pope Night even became connected to political events leading up to the Revolutionary War.  Shortly after the Boston Massacre of March 1770, for example, when Captain Preston and the British soldiers were on trial, a Catholic dimension surfaced. The Boston Gazette and other newspapers suggested that many of the accused soldiers were actually Irish Catholics, feeding into an anti-Catholic sentiment stretching back to the Puritan days.   The Providence Gazette even suggested that Pope’s Day should move from November 5 to March 5, the day of the Boston Massacre, and that Preston and his men should be added to the effigies to be burned.

It was actually General George Washington who helped set the stage for ending Pope’s Day in New England, thereby setting the stage for the eventual acceptance of Catholics in the United States.

“On taking command of the Continental forces besieging Boston in 1775, Washington was appalled at the scurrilous anti-Catholic songs being sung by some of his troops,” according to The New York Times. “The general was hoping to win the support of French Catholics in Quebec, which American rebels had invaded. Washington gave strict orders to end the celebrations.”

A General Order issued on November 5, 1775 by Washington’s command staff reads:

“…As the Commander in Chief has been apprized of a design form’d, for the observance of that ridiculous and childish Custom of burning the Effigy of the pope—He cannot help expressing his surprise that there should be Officers and Soldiers, in this army so void of common sense, as not to see the impropriety of such a step at this Juncture; at a Time when we are soliciting, and have really obtain’d, the friendship & alliance of the people of Canada, whom we ought to consider as Brethren embarked in the same Cause. The defense of the general Liberty of America: At such a juncture, and in such Circumstances, to be insulting their Religion, is so monstrous, as not to be suffered, or excused; indeed instead of offering the most remote insult, it is our duty to address public thanks to these our Brethren, as to them we are so much indebted for every late happy Success over the common Enemy in Canada.”

Later, in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania during St. Patrick’s Day, Washington learned that colonial troops, most likely Germans from Pennsylvania, were kicking around an effigy of the Pope, “causing great indignation among the Irish in the camp,” according to historian John Crimmins. Washington himself appeared at the scene and put an end to the situation, commenting in the process, “I too am a lover of St. Patrick’s Day.”

Washington and Catholicism
While George Washington was an Anglican, he had a cordial relationship with the Catholic Church and its members for many years.

He attended a Catholic service, donated money toward the construction of a Catholic church, and corresponded with the first Roman Catholic bishop in the United States. Perhaps most importantly, Washington’s statements regarding Catholicism and freedom of religion set precedents for the future of a new nation.

Anti-Catholic Oath
In the 1750s, Washington had to prove to the British government he was not Catholic and supported the Anglican Church. In both England and its American Colonies, it was common to require a religious oath to hold a rank in the military or government. The oath Washington signed stated, “I…do declare that there is no Transubstantiation in the sacrament of the Lords supper or in the Elements of Bread and wine at or after the consecration thereof by any person whatsoever.” By signing this oath, Washington was assuring the Anglican government that he was not Catholic. 

Supporting the Catholic Church
Washington socialized with prominent Catholics both at Mount Vernon and during his presidency. He attended a service at St. Mary’s Catholic Church while he was in Philadelphia for the First Continental Congress. Washington also donated money toward the construction of a Catholic church in Baltimore.

Discussing Freedom of Religion
Washington corresponded with John Carroll, who on November 14, 1789, was selected as the first Roman Catholic bishop in the United States. In March of 1790, Carroll wrote an address to Washington on behalf of the Roman Catholics in American. It was one of Carroll’s first official acts as bishop.

We have been long impatient to testify our joy and unbounded confidence, on your being called, by an unanimous vote, to the first station of a country, in which that unanimity could not have been obtained without the previous merit of unexampled services, of eminent wisdom, and unblemished virtue.… By example as well as by vigilance, you extend the influence of laws on the manners of our fellow citizens you encourage respect for religion, and inculcate, by words and actions, that principle, on which the welfare of nations so much depends, that a superintending Providence governs the events of the world, and watches over the conduct of men. Your exalted maxims and unwearied attention to the moral and physical improvement of our country have produced already the happiest effects.

George Washington to Roman Catholics in America, March 1790
…all those who conduct themselves as worthy members of the Community are equally entitled to the protection of civil Government. I hope ever to see America among the foremost nations in examples of justice and liberality. How Much Freedom Must Humanity Surrender to Survive the Intelligence It Creates?

Sam Altman has raised one of the most uncomfortable questions confronting artificial intelligence.

How much harm should society tolerate in exchange for technological freedom?

His argument acknowledges a disturbing reality.

Powerful AI models could enable sophisticated fraud, cyberattacks, manipulation, and criminal activity.

Yet restricting access could undermine innovation, individual liberty, and the democratization of intelligence.

The dilemma is profound because unrestricted access and excessive regulation both carry serious consequences.

Open AI models offer extraordinary opportunities.

They allow researchers, entrepreneurs, universities, and smaller nations to develop technologies without depending entirely on powerful corporations.
They encourage transparency, competition, and scientific discovery.

But accessibility also creates risks.

The same capabilities that help legitimate users solve complex problems could enable malicious actors to operate with greater speed, sophistication, and scale.

The question is no longer whether artificial intelligence can be misused. It is whether society can establish meaningful boundaries without surrendering the freedoms that make innovation possible.

Altman suggests that certain capabilities may become too dangerous for unrestricted access, particularly those capable of causing widespread disruption or physical harm.
That argument deserves consideration.

But it also raises another question.

Who decides where those boundaries exist?
Technology companies?
Governments?
International institutions?
Or the societies whose freedoms and security are at stake?

If a few organizations control the most powerful intelligence systems, protecting humanity could become indistinguishable from concentrating extraordinary power.
History reminds us that restrictions introduced in the name of security can outlive the threats they were intended to address.

Yet refusing safeguards could expose millions to preventable harm.
Neither extreme offers a satisfactory answer.

The challenge is to develop transparent, proportionate, and accountable safeguards that distinguish legitimate research and innovation from capabilities presenting catastrophic risks.

The greatest danger may not come exclusively from AI becoming too powerful. It may also come from allowing fear of that power to weaken the principles of an open society.
Artificial intelligence is forcing humanity to reconsider the relationship between freedom, responsibility, and collective security.

Perhaps the defining question of the AI era is not how much freedom we must surrender, but whether we can protect humanity without surrendering the very freedoms that make humanity worth protecting.

Sometimes, the problem isn't that you're not good enough. You may just be in the wrong environment.

If your business isn't growing, try a different strategy.

If your content isn't reaching people, consider changing your niche.

If your workplace doesn't value your efforts, look for somewhere your skills will be appreciated.

If your current location offers limited opportunities, consider moving somewhere with better prospects.

Don't spend your entire life trying to make things work in a place that isn't working for you.

Sometimes, you don't need to work harder. You need to change your environment.
